title: Facts and theories
summary: One test, many cases: [Theory] with [InlineData], [MemberData] and TheoryData<>, how each row shows in a report, and where table-driven tests stop helping.

steps.title: A [Theory] is one test with many rows
body: A `[Fact]` takes no parameters and is always true. A `[Theory]` is a test **with parameters**, and every data row is run (and reported) as its own test:
public void Score_maps_to_a_letter(int score, char expected)
The report shows each row with its arguments, so a failure names the exact case:

Use a theory when the **same behaviour** is checked with different inputs: boundaries of one rule, a parsing table, a list of invalid inputs. Do not use one to glue different behaviours together behind an `if` on a parameter: that is several tests pretending to be one.

steps.prompt: Turn three copy-pasted facts into one theory with three rows.
steps.explain: `[Theory]` plus one `[InlineData]` per row. The parameter names must match their use in the body (`valid`), and xUnit shows them in the report.

steps.title: When the data does not fit in an attribute: MemberData and TheoryData
body: Attribute arguments must be compile-time constants, so `decimal`, `DateOnly`, objects and lists cannot go in `[InlineData]`. Put them in a static member and point `[MemberData]` at it. `TheoryData<...>` makes the rows type-checked:
public static TheoryData<decimal, decimal> Discounts => new()
public void Ten_percent_off(decimal price, decimal expected)
Also good to know in v3:
- `MatrixTheoryData<int, string>` runs every combination of two (to five) lists.
- A row can be a `TheoryDataRow<...>` with a `Skip`, a `Label` or its own `Timeout`.
- `[MemberData]` may point at an `async` method returning `Task<...>`.
Keep tables short and readable. 40 rows of random inputs hide which case matters; that job belongs to property-based testing (module 8).

code: public void Ten_percent_off(decimal price, decimal expected) { }
options: Attribute arguments must be constants of a few simple types, and `decimal` is not one of them: use `[MemberData]` with `TheoryData<decimal, decimal>`
A theory needs at least two `[InlineData]` rows
Theories cannot have a parameter named `expected`
steps.explain: C# allows only constants of primitive types, `string`, `Type` and enums (and arrays of them) in attributes. A common workaround is `[InlineData(19.99, 17.99)]` with `double` parameters, which silently brings floating-point error into money tests. `TheoryData<decimal, decimal>` keeps the real type.

steps.prompt: Fact, InlineData theory, or MemberData theory?
items: Ten date strings that must all fail to parse
Orders built from a list of `OrderLine` objects
A new account starts with a zero balance
steps.explain: One case is a fact. Many cases of one rule with constant inputs fit `[InlineData]`; anything that is not a constant (decimal, dates, objects) needs a member.

steps.title: Every boundary in one theory
prompt: The grading service maps a score to a letter. This code is compiled beside your tests:
- one `[Theory]` with an `[InlineData]` row for **both sides of every boundary**;
- one more `[Theory]` for scores that must throw, using `Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>`.
At least **10** rows in all. Six planted bugs, each moving one edge by one point.
starter: public void Score_maps_to_a_letter(int score, char expected)
solution: public void Score_maps_to_a_letter(int score, char expected)

mutants.name: 101 is accepted
mutants.hint: Add 101 to the scores that must throw.

require.message: Checks the refused scores with Assert.Throws

hints: Each `>=` has two sides: 90 must be an A and 89 a B. Do the same for 80, 70 and 60.
The range check has two edges too: -1 and 101 must throw.
Rows: 90 A, 89 B, 80 B, 79 C, 70 C, 69 D, 60 D, 59 F, plus a throwing theory with -1 and 101.
steps.explain: Ten rows of one rule read like the specification itself, and each row fails on its own with its values in the name. Testing both sides of every `>=` is what catches the off-by-one.
